enum: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Can't tell: The paper does not report the timeline or number of meetings across the five-stage source water protection planning process, whether all six communities completed every stage, or whether any working-committee members withdrew over time (§3.2-3.3, pp. 8-9).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern for causal inference (uncontrolled qualitative design): Causal claims attributing on-reserve undrinkable water to settler-colonial legal and administrative structures rely on historical-institutional and political-ecological reasoning across six First Nation cases without a non-reserve comparator or empirical adjustment for geographic remoteness, hydrogeology, settlement density or local fiscal capacity (§2.2-2.3, pp. 4-8; §4-5, pp. 10-13).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate (narrative socio-legal contextualization): Key constitutional, treaty and statutory frameworks—Treaties 4, 5, 6 and 7, the Constitution Act, the Indian Act (1876), the Natural Resources Transfer Act (1930), provincial/municipal land-use delegation, the Crown's duty to consult and federal administrative criteria for reserve infrastructure—are coherently integrated into the institutional analysis (§2.2-2.3, pp. 4-8; §5, p. 12), though primarily via secondary scholarship rather than granular primary statutory or bylaw coding.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern / Can't tell on procedural specifics: Source-water threats were elicited through facilitated community working-committee meetings using a five-stage planning template and a likelihood-by-consequence risk-ranking matrix, alongside visual field inspection of landfills (§3.2-3.3, §4, pp. 8-11), but meeting protocols, note-taking/recording procedures and exact matrix scoring rules are unreported and no biophysical water testing was conducted.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate for perceived local risk / Weak for physical water quality: Drinking-water threats and household tap/cistern avoidance are documented via participatory risk rankings (Table 2) and field descriptions of concrete cisterns, backyard sewage 'shoot-outs' and unlined landfills (§4, pp. 10-12), without primary microbiological/chemical water sampling or systematic household survey/health data.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern: Table 2 selectively reports only the highest-ranked perceived threats per community rather than complete risk inventories or raw likelihood-consequence ratings, and no pre-specified qualitative protocol or facilitation guide is cited (§4, p. 10).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate concern / Can't tell on within-case recruitment: The six Prairie First Nation communities partnered voluntarily at each First Nation's request (§3.1, §3.3, pp. 8-9), which suits participatory case research, but the paper does not explain whether other communities were approached or excluded, how individual working-committee members were selected within each Nation or how many individuals participated.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was there a clear statement of the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper clearly states both its overarching governance question—examining the role of political structures and colonial institutions in excluding Indigenous peoples from water governance in Canada—and its empirical case-study objective of identifying local risks to drinking water sources across six Prairie First Nations through a political ecology lens.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF p. 1 (Abstract), p. 2 (§1 Introduction), and p. 8 (§3.1 Study Area)

domain_ratings.justification: A qualitative, community-based participatory case-study methodology combined with political ecology institutional analysis is appropriate for investigating community-identified threats to drinking water and understanding the socio-political and historical governance relations underlying on-reserve water insecurity.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the research design appropriate to address the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: Using a multiple-case design across six Prairie First Nations spanning Treaties 4, 5, 6 and 7 embedded in a structured five-stage Source Water Protection (SWP) planning process—paired with Robbins's political ecology narratives—logically connects local infrastructure realities to macro-level colonial governance structures, though explicit justification for selecting six cases rather than an alternative design is brief.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the recruitment strategy appropriate to the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: While the authors state that each of the six First Nations partnered voluntarily at the community's own request and that working committees comprised elected officials, administrators, water treatment plant operators, Elders and community members, the paper provides no details on how individual committee members were recruited, how many participants served on each committee or whether key perspectives were missing.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 8-9 (§3.1 Study Area, §3.3 Data Collection)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data collected in a way that addressed the research issue?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper outlines the five-stage SWP planning framework, facilitation of working-committee meetings by the lead author, a likelihood-by-consequence risk-ranking matrix and visual inspection of community landfills (with photographs), but omits critical procedural details including dates and frequency of meetings, how deliberations were recorded (e.g. audio transcripts vs. facilitator notes), exact matrix scoring criteria and how household water avoidance claims were documented.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Has the relationship between researcher and participants been adequately considered?
domain_ratings.justification: Section 3.4 ('Statement of Positionality') explicitly reflects on the authors' status as non-Indigenous university researchers working within a power-laden settler-colonial context, discloses their prior community-based water research history since 2013/2015, acknowledges institutional histories of unethical Indigenous research and states that the authors do not claim to speak as the 'voice' of First Nation communities.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Have ethical issues been taken into consideration?
domain_ratings.justification: Although community engagement occurred voluntarily at each First Nation's request, community names are anonymized by Treaty area in Figure 1 and Table 2, and §3.4 acknowledges historical ethical failures in research with Indigenous peoples, the paper reports no institutional Research Ethics Board (REB) approval, formal band council research agreements, Indigenous data-governance (e.g. OCAP) arrangements or individual informed consent procedures.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 8-10 (§3.1, §3.3-3.4, Figure 1, Table 2) and p. 13 (Acknowledgments)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data analysis sufficiently rigorous?
domain_ratings.justification: Beyond noting that committee-reported threats were categorized via a likelihood-times-consequence risk-ranking matrix and deductively interpreted through Robbins's four political ecology narratives (selecting 'degradation and marginalization'), the authors provide no explanation of qualitative coding or thematic synthesis across the six cases, no participant quotes and no member-checking or triangulation procedures to guard against facilitator/analytic bias.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 3-4 (§2.1, Table 1) and pp. 10-13 (§4 Results, Table 2, §5 Discussion and Conclusions)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there a clear statement of findings?
domain_ratings.justification: Findings are clearly organized around cross-community high-risk threats to drinking water (Table 2)—most prominently household concrete cisterns/truck delivery, backyard sewage 'shoot-outs' and unlined open landfills—and are coherently tied back to the research question regarding federal infrastructure design and colonial exclusion of First Nations from land and water governance.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 10-13 (§4 Results, Table 2, §5 Discussion and Conclusions)

domain_ratings.justification: Narrative assessment: The study makes a valuable empirical and conceptual contribution by documenting recurring, state-designed on-reserve water and sanitation vulnerabilities across six Prairie First Nations (cistern delivery bottlenecks, surface sewage 'shoot-outs' and unlined landfills) and reframing technical 'water problems' as governance injustices rooted in Indian Act and constitutional-jurisdictional exclusion, while pointing toward household water insecurity and Indigenous self-determination frameworks for policy reform.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Baijius and Patrick (2019) present a participatory qualitative multiple-case study of source water protection (SWP) planning across six First Nation communities in the Canadian Prairies (Treaties 4, 5, 6 and 7), interpreted through Robbins's political ecology framework of degradation and marginalization. Methodological strengths under the CASP Qualitative Checklist include clearly articulated research aims (Q1), an appropriate qualitative participatory case design linking local infrastructure vulnerabilities to colonial water governance (Q2, Q3), an explicit and thoughtful researcher positionality statement addressing settler-colonial power dynamics (Q6), and a clear synthesis of recurring on-reserve water risks—household water cisterns, backyard sewage 'shoot-outs' and unlined landfills—and their roots in federal Indian Act control and jurisdictional exclusion (Q9, Q10). However, transparency on empirical execution is limited across four CASP domains rated 'Can't tell': within-community participant recruitment and sample sizes are omitted (Q4); meeting counts, data recording/note-taking procedures and exact risk-matrix scoring rules are unreported (Q5); formal Research Ethics Board approval, community research protocols and informed consent procedures are not stated despite working with Indigenous communities (Q7); and qualitative analytic/coding and validation procedures are not described (Q8). Overall methodological concern is therefore rated Moderate (4 Can't tell / 0 No items).
raw_response.overall_rating: Moderate concern (4 Can't tell / 0 No items)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Participatory qualitative multiple-case study (community-based source water protection planning workshops and field observations across six Prairie First Nation communities, framed by political ecology)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Research question and theoretical framing: §1-2 (PDF pp. 1-8); empirical case-study design, study locations, SWP framework, working-committee data collection and researcher positionality: §3.1-3.4 (PDF pp. 8-10, Figures 1-2); risk-ranking outputs and field descriptions of cisterns, sewage 'shoot-outs' and landfills: §4 (PDF pp. 10-12, Table 2, Figures 3-4); synthesis linking empirical risks to Indian Act / colonial governance: §5 (PDF pp. 12-13); funding/acknowledgments: PDF p. 13.
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The empirical component of the study (§3-4, PDF pp. 8-12) consists of primary community-based participatory qualitative case studies across six First Nation communities using facilitated working-committee workshops, qualitative categorical risk rankings (Table 2) and visual field inspections of water/waste infrastructure, coupled with a researcher positionality statement (§3.4). Because the likelihood-by-consequence planning heuristic yields only qualitative threat categories in Table 2 without quantitative sample data or statistical analysis, MMAT does not apply; and because the study conducts primary fieldwork with human community committees rather than purely doctrinal or archival legal-historical analysis, the CASP Qualitative Checklist is the single best-fitting official instrument.
